article.title: Perforce's TotalView Debugger Adds Python Support for Parallel HPC Applications, Shown at SC26
article.summary: Perforce's TotalView debugger now supports Python in its latest quarterly release, using Microsoft's debugpy backend, demonstrated at the SC26 conference in Chicago.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

Perforce Software used the SC26 supercomputing conference in Chicago this week to demonstrate that its TotalView parallel debugger now supports Python, according to [The Register](https://www.theregister.com/devops/2026/11/17/python-parallel-debugging-comes-to-hpc-thanks-to-totalview-upgrade/5310564). The conference, officially titled "The International Conference for High Performance Computing, Networking, Storage, and Analysis," runs November 15-20, 2026, in Chicago, Illinois, according to the [SC26 conference site](https://sc26.supercomputing.org/). Perforce showed the feature at booth #2829, as reported by [The Register](https://www.theregister.com/devops/2026/11/17/python-parallel-debugging-comes-to-hpc-thanks-to-totalview-upgrade/5310564).

TotalView has historically supported only C/C++ and Fortran; the Python support arrived in what The Register describes as the tool's "latest quarterly release." Perforce's own [product page](https://www.perforce.com/products/totalview) confirms the feature is live, advertising "Parallel Python Debugging Now Available in TotalView."

## What We Know

TotalView was built in the late 1980s for military applications and today mainly serves developers in high-performance computing, where large scientific applications run in parallel across thousands or tens of thousands of processes, according to [The Register](https://www.theregister.com/devops/2026/11/17/python-parallel-debugging-comes-to-hpc-thanks-to-totalview-upgrade/5310564). Perforce acquired TotalView in 2019 as part of its purchase of Rogue Wave Software, the outlet reported.

Bill Burns, Perforce's vice president of software engineering, told The Register that "Python has grown in popularity" in the HPC community. The mpi4py library, which TotalView now supports alongside Python's built-in multiprocessing module, bridges Python programs to the Message Passing Interface standard that lets different parts of an application running on different hardware communicate, per [The Register](https://www.theregister.com/devops/2026/11/17/python-parallel-debugging-comes-to-hpc-thanks-to-totalview-upgrade/5310564).

Burns described the core pitch for TotalView's approach to debugging at scale: "Even if you have 10,000 things going on, if you have one crash in there, TotalView can pinpoint that," he said, adding that the tool can inspect the state of a process, its threads, or the GPU it is using, as reported by [The Register](https://www.theregister.com/devops/2026/11/17/python-parallel-debugging-comes-to-hpc-thanks-to-totalview-upgrade/5310564).

Under the hood, TotalView uses Microsoft's debugpy engine, accessed through the Debug Adapter Protocol, to power a hierarchical tree server that aggregates hundreds of stack traces into a single view and highlights the ones that fall outside expected bounds, according to [The Register](https://www.theregister.com/devops/2026/11/17/python-parallel-debugging-comes-to-hpc-thanks-to-totalview-upgrade/5310564). A developer can launch a single-process or parallel Python program under TotalView's control, set breakpoints, inspect variables and data structures, and evaluate Python expressions, the outlet reported. Perforce's product page separately describes the ability to "view and control multiple Python processes at once while you debug a distributed application."

Burns pointed to the removal of Python's global interpreter lock as a factor driving demand for better Python debugging tools in HPC. "If you have a CPU with 64 cores, you can run 64 independent threads all working in unison on that CPU. Without GIL, those threads will run fully asynchronously," he said, according to [The Register](https://www.theregister.com/devops/2026/11/17/python-parallel-debugging-comes-to-hpc-thanks-to-totalview-upgrade/5310564). The Register ties this to Python 3.14, noting the release added the ability to use concurrent interpreters alongside free-threading support. Python's own [release notes](https://docs.python.org/3.14/whatsnew/3.14.html) specify that free-threaded mode was initially added in Python 3.13 and was "significantly improved" and made officially supported in 3.14, while the new `concurrent.interpreters` standard-library module is new to 3.14. More concurrency also means more ways for things to go wrong, Burns said: "Now you're going to end up with lock and thread contention and race conditions and all the things that C++ and Fortran developers have dealt with for years."

The product is not yet a full cross-language debugger. The Register reported that developers currently have to choose between debugging the C/C++ side of an application, while viewing the Python stack, or debugging the Python side on its own — Burns said Perforce plans to merge both modes into a single workflow in a future release. TotalView currently supports mpi4py and Python's multiprocessing module out of the box; Burns said future releases will add support for other Python concurrency frameworks, including Dask and PyTorch's torchrun, per [The Register](https://www.theregister.com/devops/2026/11/17/python-parallel-debugging-comes-to-hpc-thanks-to-totalview-upgrade/5310564). TotalView is priced on a token-based model, in which each token buys the capability to debug one process, the outlet reported.

## What We Don't Know

Neither Perforce's product page nor The Register's report gives a specific version number for the "latest quarterly release" that added Python support, or a firm date for when the cross-language merge, Dask support, or torchrun support will ship. Pricing details beyond the token-based model — such as the cost per token — were not disclosed in either source.

## Analysis

The move extends a decades-old, military-rooted parallel debugger into a language it was never built for, reflecting how Python's use in HPC has grown alongside scientific computing and distributed AI training workloads that increasingly mix Python front ends with C/C++ or Fortran performance-critical code, according to [The Register](https://www.theregister.com/devops/2026/11/17/python-parallel-debugging-comes-to-hpc-thanks-to-totalview-upgrade/5310564).
